entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Pomponius Flaccus was a prominent Roman senator who played a crucial role in the reign of Emperor Tiberius (14-37 CE) in Rome, Italy. He held the office of consul in AD 17, alongside Gaius Caelius Rufus, and served as a governor in several provinces, including Asia Minor and Syria.

Flaccus was a key figure in the Roman imperial system, serving as a legate under Tiberius and later as a consul, and was known for his administrative skills and his ability to navigate the complexities of imperial politics. He was also a member of the Roman aristocracy and held significant influence in Rome's social and political circles.

Flaccus's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as he played a key role in shaping the Roman Empire's governance and administration, and his experiences as a senator and governor provide valuable insights into the workings of the Roman imperial system.

The year 33 CE marks the end of Flaccus's life, but his impact on Roman history continued, influencing the development of the Roman Empire and the subsequent rise of Christianity.

The legacy of Lucius Pomponius Flaccus is a testament to the enduring power of Roman politics and the importance of understanding the intricate web of alliances and rivalries that shaped the empire's rise and fall.
